learning.title: Count against both parents before unioning a conflict block, because the union of two ones is two
learning.trigger: Resolving a git merge conflict in a file where both sides look additive - separate routes, separate keys, separate entries - so the obvious resolution is to keep both.
learning.rule: A conflict block can cut INSIDE a body. Two blocks that look like independent additions may be the head and tail of one definition that both parents already had exactly once. Concatenating them yields a truncated definition followed by a complete duplicate, and the syntax error appears at the seam rather than where the damage is.

For every name the resolution touches, count its occurrences in both parents and in the result before believing the resolution: `git show HEAD:file | grep -c`, `git show origin/main:file | grep -c`, then the working file. Ours one, theirs one, result two means the block was not additive - the union duplicated an existing definition. Counting beats reading the diff and guessing, because the guess is what produced the duplication.

The formatter hides syntax breaks. `deno fmt` reported a genuinely unparseable file as "Found 1 not formatted file", so a fmt failure on a file just resolved by hand should be read as possible syntax damage, not as whitespace drift: run the type checker or a parser against that file specifically before running the formatter again. The compiler names the line; the formatter names the symptom.

verification.requirement: Record the occurrence count of each touched name in both parents and in the resolved file, and the exact command that proved the file parses. A conflict resolved by eye and confirmed only by fmt is treated as unresolved.
